items.followUp: Why can the particles of a suspension be separated by filtration?

rubric.why: Identifies that a suspension is not uniform throughout.
rubric.description: States that a suspension is heterogeneous and its particles are not uniformly distributed.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the suspended particles do not form a uniform mixture or solution.

rubric.why: Explains how the particles cause the mixture to remain non-uniform.
rubric.description: States that suspension particles settle on standing, making the composition uneven.
rubric.how: Award for linking settling of the particles with uneven distribution.

modelAnswer: A suspension is heterogeneous because its particles do not dissolve and are not uniformly distributed throughout the mixture.
The particles settle on standing, so the composition is uneven.

items.followUp: What is an alloy? Give one example other than brass.

rubric.why: Gives the defining composition of an alloy.
rubric.description: Defines an alloy as a mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal.
rubric.how: Award for identifying an alloy as a mixture and mentioning its metallic components.

rubric.why: Provides a correct example and its constituents.
rubric.description: Gives brass as an example, made from copper and zinc.
rubric.how: Award for the correct example with both constituent elements.

modelAnswer: An alloy is a mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal.
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

items.followUp: Why is potassium more reactive than silver?

rubric.why: Relates the low reactivity of silver and gold to their tendency to form ions.
rubric.description: States that silver and gold do not readily lose electrons.
rubric.how: Award for explaining their low tendency to lose electrons.

rubric.why: Connects their electron-loss tendency to their observed chemical behaviour.
rubric.description: Concludes that silver and gold have low chemical reactivity.
rubric.how: Award for stating that they react less readily than more reactive metals.

modelAnswer: Silver and gold have a low tendency to lose electrons.
Therefore, they have low chemical reactivity and do not react readily with other substances.

items.followUp: Define chemistry and explain any three of its branches.

rubric.why: Covers the main subject matter included in the definition of chemistry.
rubric.description: Defines chemistry as the study of the composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes it undergoes.
rubric.how: Award for a definition that includes matter and its composition, properties or changes.

rubric.why: Identifies the subject matter of organic chemistry.
rubric.description: Explains that organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Award for naming carbon compounds as the focus of this branch.

rubric.why: Identifies the subject matter of inorganic chemistry.
rubric.description: Explains that inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, apart from most carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Award for describing the study of elements or inorganic compounds.

rubric.why: Identifies the focus of physical chemistry.
rubric.description: Explains that physical chemistry studies the physical properties of matter and the laws governing chemical changes.
rubric.how: Award for linking physical chemistry with physical properties or laws governing chemical processes.

rubric.why: Identifies the focus of biochemistry.
rubric.description: Explains that biochemistry studies the chemicals and reactions occurring in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award for relating this branch to chemical substances or reactions in living things.

modelAnswer: Chemistry is the study of the composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes it undergoes.
Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds.
Inorganic chemistry is the study of elements and their compounds, other than most carbon compounds.
Physical chemistry studies the physical properties of matter and the laws governing chemical changes.
Biochemistry is the study of chemicals and chemical reactions in living organisms.

items.followUp: State two differences between the energy levels of an atom and the spaces between them.

rubric.why: States that electrons occupy specified energy levels around the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in definite orbits or shells, each with a fixed energy.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning definite electron orbits or shells with fixed energy.

rubric.why: Describes the energy behaviour of electrons while they remain in an allowed orbit.
rubric.description: States that an electron does not radiate or absorb energy while in a stationary orbit.
rubric.how: Award for stating that energy is not exchanged while the electron remains in its orbit.

rubric.why: Explains that an electron changes energy by moving between allowed orbits.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs or releases energy when it jumps between energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for explaining energy absorption or release during a transition between shells.

rubric.why: Relates the energy exchanged to the separation between the levels.
rubric.description: States that the absorbed or emitted energy equals the difference between the two energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for linking the energy of the transition to the difference between the levels.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in definite circular orbits or shells, each having a fixed energy.
An electron does not radiate or absorb energy while it remains in a stationary orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to jump to a higher energy level and releases energy when it falls to a lower level.
The energy absorbed or emitted is equal to the difference between the two energy levels.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature and particle size affect diffusion in liquids.

rubric.why: Describes the effect of temperature on particle motion and diffusion.
rubric.description: States that increasing temperature increases the rate of diffusion.
rubric.how: Award for correctly linking higher temperature with faster diffusion.

rubric.why: Describes the effect of the concentration difference on diffusion.
rubric.description: States that a greater concentration difference causes faster diffusion.
rubric.how: Award for relating a steeper concentration difference to an increased diffusion rate.

rubric.why: Describes how particle size affects the rate of diffusion.
rubric.description: States that smaller particles diffuse faster than larger particles.
rubric.how: Award for correctly comparing diffusion rates for small and large particles.

rubric.why: Describes how resistance to particle movement in the liquid affects diffusion.
rubric.description: States that diffusion is faster in a less viscous liquid.
rubric.how: Award for linking lower viscosity with less resistance and faster diffusion.

modelAnswer: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so diffusion occurs faster.
A greater concentration difference between regions increases the rate of diffusion.
Smaller particles diffuse faster than larger particles.
Diffusion occurs faster in a less viscous liquid because the particles move with less resistance.

items.followUp: What is the Tyndall effect, and which type of mixture shows it?

rubric.why: Describes the apparent and actual nature of colloids.
rubric.description: States that colloids are heterogeneous mixtures, although they may appear homogeneous.
rubric.how: Award for distinguishing their actual heterogeneous nature from their appearance.

rubric.why: Identifies a characteristic interaction of colloidal particles with light.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles scatter light, producing the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award for stating that colloids scatter a beam of light.

rubric.why: Describes the stability of colloidal particles in the mixture.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles do not settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award for correctly stating that the particles remain dispersed on standing.

rubric.why: Describes how colloidal particles behave during ordinary filtration.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.
rubric.how: Award for distinguishing colloid particles from larger suspension particles in filtration.

modelAnswer: A colloid is heterogeneous, although it may appear homogeneous.
Colloidal particles scatter light and show the Tyndall effect.
Colloidal particles do not settle on standing.
They cannot be separated from the dispersion by ordinary filtration.

items.followUp: What fraction of the mass of a carbon-12 atom is one atomic mass unit?

rubric.why: Gives the standard definition of the atomic mass unit.
rubric.description: Defines one atomic mass unit as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.how: Award for the correct one-twelfth reference to carbon-12.

rubric.why: Explains why a convenient unit is used for atomic masses.
rubric.description: States that atomic masses are extremely small, so the atomic mass unit provides a convenient unit for expressing them.
rubric.how: Award for explaining the need for a convenient unit because atomic masses are very small.

modelAnswer: One atomic mass unit (1 u) is one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
It is needed because the actual masses of atoms are extremely small, so expressing them in a convenient unit is easier.
